mcqs.question: What's the expected default approach to cross-service consistency, and when is the exception justified?
options: Default to sagas with compensating actions, reserving 2PC for a small, tightly-coupled, low-latency set of participants with a genuine atomicity need
Always use 2PC for any operation touching more than one service
Avoid any cross-service consistency mechanism entirely
Let each service handle failures independently with no coordination at all
mcqs.explanation: The senior default is sagas, with 2PC reserved for the narrow case of few, co-located participants and a real atomicity requirement. Defaulting to 2PC everywhere ignores its availability cost; ignoring coordination entirely risks genuinely inconsistent outcomes the business cares about.

mcqs.question: Why does 2PC's lock-hold duration create a throughput ceiling that adding app servers can't fix?
options: It has no effect on throughput since databases handle locks for free
Each participant holding locks for the full round-trip duration caps throughput on that data, regardless of how many app servers are added
It only affects latency, never throughput
It only matters if there are more than 100 participants
mcqs.explanation: Since every participant holds its lock for the entire 2PC round trip, the data itself — not the number of app servers — becomes the bottleneck; more app servers just queue up behind the same held locks. Locks aren't free, the effect shows up as a throughput ceiling (not only latency), and it applies even with just two participants.

mcqs.question: What's the core trade-off between 2PC and sagas?
options: 2PC and sagas provide identical guarantees, so the choice is arbitrary
Sagas provide stronger atomicity guarantees than 2PC
2PC gives true atomicity at the cost of availability; sagas give availability at the cost of instantly-visible atomicity
Neither approach can handle a partial failure of any kind
mcqs.explanation: 2PC's blocking protocol buys real, instant atomicity but risks availability if the coordinator stalls; sagas keep every step independently available but allow a transient in-between state visible to the outside. Sagas don't out-atomicity 2PC, and both approaches do have defined ways of handling partial failure.

mcqs.question: What's wrong with reaching for a distributed transaction as the first idea whenever multiple services are touched?
options: 2PC is always faster than a saga for any number of participants
Sagas cannot be used for financial transactions under any circumstances
2PC has no failure modes that need special handling
Reaching for 2PC first, before checking whether eventual correctness with compensation is enough, trades away availability the feature may not have needed to give up
mcqs.explanation: Most features tolerate a brief transient state, which a saga already handles safely — reaching for 2PC by default pays its availability cost without checking whether it was actually needed. 2PC is not faster in general, sagas are used for financial flows all the time, and 2PC has real failure modes (like a crashed coordinator) that need explicit handling.
